summary:
Field Shift is a web app that helps a farmer decide what to grow next on a specific field. The farmer spins a globe, clicks the outline of their field (boundaries from Fields of the World), and enters the crops grown in the last three years. The app then combines long-term climate from NASA POWER, soil properties from ISRIC SoilGrids and terrain data to explain, in plain language with the numbers behind it, which crops fit the field, which to avoid and why.

It addresses the challenge by comparing three rotation strategies, including the farmer's current one, and by stating for each the reasons, evidence, benefits, risks and data gaps. Crop requirements come from the FAO EcoCrop database; rotation rules follow published agronomy guides. The app also screens climate stress: dryness, excess water, freezing months and soil acidity.

It matters because rotation decisions are usually made from habit, while climate is shifting. Field Shift turns open NASA and partner data into advice a non-specialist can read in minutes, in English and Ukrainian. It never promises yields, shows its confidence level, and reminds the user to confirm with a local agronomist.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

On a 3D satellite globe with country and region borders and place names, the farmer zooms in and clicks the outline of their field; if no outline exists, the clicked point is used. They then choose what grew there in each of the last three years. Field Shift returns what to sow next year with suggested area shares, what not to sow and why, an indicative growing season for each crop, and three three-year rotation strategies: the current practice, a balanced plan and a soil-first plan.

HOW IT WORKS

For the chosen location the server collects monthly climate normals from NASA POWER at nine sample points inside a radius, topsoil properties from ISRIC SoilGrids, and elevation and slope. The logic derives the Koppen climate class, potential evapotranspiration (Hargreaves-Samani) and an aridity index. Each of 25 crops is scored against FAO EcoCrop limits for temperature, annual rainfall and soil pH; the weakest factor decides. Rotation rules lower the score of a crop repeated from last year or from the same botanical family, and favour a legume when none was grown. Four stress indicators are screened: dryness, excess water, freezing months and soil acidity.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

A non-specialist gets field-specific, explained advice in minutes, in English or Ukrainian, with nothing to install. Every recommendation shows its numbers, sources, confidence and data gaps, so it supports a conversation with a local agronomist rather than replacing one. The aim is more diverse rotations that protect soil and spread climate risk.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React, Vite, MapLibre GL with globe projection, PMTiles, Hono on the Cloudflare Workers runtime, Vitest (110 automated tests), npm workspaces, GitHub pull requests. Data: NASA POWER, ISRIC SoilGrids, Fields of the World, OpenStreetMap, FAO EcoCrop, Esri World Imagery. An AI assistant (Claude) was used for coding and review.

CREATIVITY

The farmer selects a real field outline on a globe instead of typing coordinates. Advice is written as short everyday sentences that keep the numbers. The app says what not to sow, and why, not only what to sow. A shared, versioned API contract with automatic checks let the team build map, interface, server and agronomy logic in parallel.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Honesty about limits came first. The app never predicts yield or income and never gives a sowing date. Heat and erosion risk are reported as "not assessed" because we have no validated thresholds. Crop limits are species-level, not variety-level, and irrigation is not modelled. Rotation penalty weights are our own heuristics and are labelled as such. Sources that are not NASA are named as such. When a data source fails, the app says so and lowers its confidence instead of inventing values.
